title: I wrote the story for a Monkey Island-style adventure and had AI build the engine and assets
author: Ok-Spend5655
selftext:
Hi everyone, I wanted to get some honest feedback on Twenty to Four, a point-and-click detective comedy I made as part of my HeyBotcha YouTube series testing AI game-making.



I wrote and edited the story. AI made the engine and assets, with very, very minor fixes from me. I was aiming for that classic early-90s LucasArts feel, especially Monkey Island 1 and 2, with plenty of humour and puzzles.



You play Ambrose Tully, a detective working through a missing-person case across nine chapters. I’m curious how it holds up as an actual game, beyond the fact that AI was used to make it.



If you give it a try, see if you can beat the whole thing. It’s free on CrazyGames. There are hints in Tully’s notebook if you get stuck, unlocked by watching a short ad.



Full free game: [https://www.crazygames.com/game/twenty-to-four](https://www.crazygames.com/game/twenty-to-four)



What worked for you, and what would you change? I’m especially interested in whether the puzzles feel fair, whether the humour lands, and where you get stuck. For anyone else developing with AI, how much manual fixing have you needed?

comments.author: ALbera_Uhata
comments.body: Hello, could you please tell me what tools were used in the AI ​​creation?

replies.author: Ok-Spend5655
replies.body:
Hi! Mainly Claude Opus 5.5 for the engine and assets. Two close-up images started as ChatGPT art, which Claude converted into the game’s pixel style. I wrote and edited the story.



Opus also built me a sprite editor so I could override sprite animations, which I used a few times.
